title: Start a nail by holding it while tapping it in, then drive it home
instruction: Drive the nail into the board at the pencil mark.
context: Driving a nail is one of the most familiar household jobs: hanging a picture, fixing a loose board, putting up a shelf. The US Army and Air Force hand-tool manual (TM 9-243 / TO 32-1-101) gives the procedure: "Support a common nail between thumb and first finger about halfway up the nail. Tap nail head with hammer face until the nail will remain standing by itself. Remove fingers and drive nail flush." A nail stood on its point falls over as soon as it is let go, so one hand has to hold it upright on its mark while the other taps it in until it stands by itself; then the holding hand has to get out of the hammer's way before the nail is driven home. The instruction only says to drive the nail in at the mark.
setup: A table in front of two arms (bases 61 cm apart), seen by one overhead camera and a camera on each wrist. Positions are in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases: x forward (away from the arms), y to the robot's left. A 25 cm offcut of western red cedar 2x6 (3.8 x 14 cm) stands on its narrow edge (x 19.1 to 22.9, y -7.8 to 17.2), held to the table by two steel angle brackets; a pencil cross on its top edge, 14 cm above the table, marks where the nail goes (x 21.0, y 4.7). A 4d finishing nail (38 mm under its head, 1.8 mm shank, 2.4 mm head, 0.8 g) lies on the table beyond the board's left end, along x, its point toward the arms at x 17.0, y 24.2. A 7 oz claw hammer with a hickory handle (Stanley 51-613: 198 g head, 23 mm face, 29 cm long, 0.34 kg in all) lies on its side on the table to the right, its head at x 10.1, y -10.7 and its handle running back to the right. The board is fixed; the nail and the hammer are loose. The layout is the same in every trial, as in the screenshot.
scoring: The bodies' poses are read from the simulation, and each gripper's shape from the arm's joints. The nail's way into the wood is a model: its point is held where it touches the wood at the mark, and it sinks only when the hammer's face strikes its head at 0.3 m/s or more, each blow until the wood's resistance R(d) = 5.7 N/mm x (depth + 2 mm) has taken 0.7 x the hammer's kinetic energy; a steady push never drives it; until it is 5.5 mm in it falls over unless held, and from then on it stands at the lean it has; a blow more than 15 deg off the nail's axis bends it. A bent nail, or the hammer striking a gripper other than the one holding it (for example the one holding the nail), scores 0 for the rest of the run. Otherwise partial credit is the best stage reached: 0.25 the nail started at the mark (2 mm or more in, its point within 3 mm of the cross's middle); 0.5 standing on its own at the mark (8 mm or more in, upright within 5 deg, no gripper touching it); 0.75 driven home (its head flush with the wood within 1 mm, upright within 5 deg, at the mark, no gripper touching it). 1.0: that, with the hammer let go and at rest and both grippers 5 cm or more from the nail, still for 1 s. Doing nothing scores 0. On a real board each is checked with a ruler and a square: the point's distance from the cross, the head's height above the wood, the nail's lean against a square while it stands, and a ruler across the head touching the wood on both sides when it is home.
reset_notes: Real board, before every trial: a fresh 25 cm offcut of cedar 2x6 held on edge by the two brackets at the same place on the table, a pencil cross drawn across its top edge at its middle, a new 4d finishing nail laid on the table and the hammer laid on its side, as in the screenshot. Simulation: each trial starts the simulator afresh (each inspect-robots run does).
fidelity: Rigid bodies in Isaac Sim 6.1 (PhysX), 20 Hz control. The nail's way into the wood is a model, not contact: under the mark the board's collision is open and a joint holds the nail's point and depth; each blow drives it until the Wood Handbook's resistance has taken 0.7 of its energy (numbers to be measured on the real board). A bent nail is scored but not shown bent; the wood does not split.
scores: Dream-1 run: 0.0 (the right gripper hovered over the hammer's handle with its fingers closed and the left over the board; nothing was picked up and the nail stayed on the table); demo: 1.0
